card_quote: What matters to her: accuracy and sources she can show students; age-appropriate stories; something that takes 5 minutes. / Teaches students to check sources; collects questions that start an argument.
how_read: Read the how-to-play page first, then turned to the back to see if there was anything for a classroom. Went through Rounds 1 and 2 properly with a pen, then picked through the rest over about a week looking for warm-ups I could use with seventh to tenth graders, skipping most of the physics and maths. Ended at the 'Using this book in class' page.

w1_friction.note: Only the score table and scoresheet can be copied for the classroom. I can't photocopy a story page for my kids, which is the whole use for me.
w1_friction.quote: The score table and team scoresheet may be copied

w1_friction.note: Drafted with AI. I'd want to check a few against the sources before I put any of it on a slide with my name on it.
w1_friction.quote: the entries were drafted with AI tools

w1_friction.note: Cute, but I'm the one who tells kids not to repeat things. A bit pleased with itself.
w1_friction.quote: Don't be the one at the table who repeats it.

w1_friction.note: Newton's apple is FOLKLORE here and then TRUE two pages later. My students would say which one is it? I'd have to explain the difference between the apple and the bump every time.
w1_friction.quote: An apple dropped onto Newton’s head

w1_friction.note: Went off into a Latin motto and the rule of three. I wanted to know what Churchill said and moved on.
w1_friction.quote: everything that comes in threes is perfect

w1_friction.note: This is the Hanlon page again with Napoleon's name on it. Two entries for one quote.
w1_friction.quote: Napoleon is not in the chain.

w1_friction.note: Good content on Stanford prison, but it name-drops Abu Ghraib and abuse. I'd cut those lines for a middle school room.
Question numbered 31 again, and headed Discovery Stories in the middle of Round 4. The contents didn't list it. Looks like a page got stuck in.
The stamp says TRUE and the text says Franklin never flew the kite. That is the one story every kid has heard, and the page contradicts itself with one thin source. I would be embarrassed to use it.
w1_friction.quote: Franklin never flew a kite in a thunderstorm

w1_friction.note: Uses the word Eskimo all through with no note. I'd need to explain that before reading it to a class.
w1_friction.quote: Eskimo languages have a great many words for snow

w1_friction.note: No way. This reads like a journal abstract. Not one kid in my building could get through it.
w1_friction.quote: orders of magnitude beyond the putative three-second window

w1_friction.note: Every other page gives me names and dates. This one says 'various laboratory studies'. Not a source I can show anyone.
Fifteen minutes a story is too long for my five-minute opener, and there's no answer key or short version. Nice idea, thin on actual help.
w1_friction.quote: A lesson can take one story in about fifteen minutes

w1_best.why: Galileo's tower is something my eighth graders already 'know', so it makes a ready bell-ringer, and the ramp and water clock part is something I can actually draw on the board.
Kitty Genovese. Students repeat the 38 witnesses line and the page gives me a real source to put on the board. I'd soften the subject for the younger classes.
Magna Carta and habeas corpus sit right in my curriculum, and 'precursor is not the same as source' is a good argument starter.
Eisenhower's own words, 'what you would call', are a primary-source clue the kids can find themselves in the transcript.
Everyone has heard Eureka in the bath. A very easy first question that shows how a story outruns its source.

w1_flat.why: Fourier transforms and conjugate variables. Lost me and would lose every kid I teach.
Leading digits of logarithm tables. Clever, but nothing to argue about in a history room.
Primes and zeta functions. Nowhere near my subject or my students.
Software project management. Why is it in a classroom book?
Goodhart and monetary policy. I read it twice and still couldn't give it to a sixteen-year-old in five minutes.

w1_review.headline: Useful bell-ringers, but check it before you put it in front of a class
w1_review.body: The format of guess first, then turn the page is just what I do at the start of a lesson, and the history and psychology stories (Genovese, Stanford prison, Magna Carta, the dominoes) will get kids arguing. Some pages are too heavy for middle school, a few pages contradict themselves or look unfinished, and I can't photocopy any of it. Bottom line: good source of questions for a teacher who checks it first, not something to hand to students as is.

w2_review_first: If a colleague asked, I'd say it's a good pile of questions for the first five minutes of class, especially the history and psychology ones. But I'd tell her to read it with a pencil, because a couple of pages are odd and a few are too grown-up or too technical for kids.

w2_lost.why: The uncertainty principle page was all maths language. I put it down and went to the next round.
Fermat and the margin. Interesting but it's maths history, and I wasn't going to use it.
Hanlon, Heinlein, a 1980 joke book. Too many names for one saying, and then Napoleon repeats it.
Stopped and stared at the kite page because it says TRUE and says the opposite.

w2_read_aloud.why: The Irish famine is in my unit, and I had no idea the textbook potato example had been discredited. Great one for a table.
Everyone at a table thinks they know this one, so it gets the loudest reaction.
Four items, not three, and a short quote everybody can say along with.
Noble savage is a phrase half the table will pin on Rousseau, and the answer is a good surprise.
Gets people talking about Vietnam, and the 'what you would call' detail is satisfying.

w2_cut.why: The Franklin kite page: wrong round, repeats a number, and the verdict and text disagree. Fix or drop it.
The goldfish page, written like a lab report with no real sources. Nobody could read it aloud.
Moore's law and chips. Nothing a room of teenagers will argue about.
Gauss and primes. Too narrow for a general quiz.
KISS. Soft verdict, little to hang a discussion on.

w2_book2: If the next one has no teacher pages I can copy, repeats the same kind of unfinished entries, or is pitched over the heads of kids.
